sections.title: Hook & Intuition (1 min)
sections.content: Introduce the challenge: Given any simple closed curve (like a rubber band on a table), can we always find four points on it that form a square? Show a circle (easy) vs. a jagged, irregular squiggle (the challenge).
sections.example: Visualize a rubber band being stretched into a random, messy shape; can we always 'pin' four points to form a perfect square?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Configuration Space (1 min)
sections.content: Define the mathematical space. We map pairs of points on the curve (x, y) to a 2D surface (a Möbius strip or a square with identified edges). This topological space helps us visualize all possible pairs of points.
sections.example: Imagine a 2D grid representing all pairs of points (s, t) on the curve; points near the diagonal represent points close together on the curve.

sections.title: Topological Mapping (1.5 min)
sections.content: Explain the 'midpoint' and 'distance' functions. We construct a continuous function from the configuration space into R². By the Intermediate Value Theorem (or Borsuk-Ulam theorem), if a function changes sign across a boundary, it must hit zero.
sections.example: Use a character, 'Topologist Tim', sliding two calipers along the curve. He marks the center and the distance; where these functions intersect zero, he finds his square's vertices.

sections.title: The Symmetry Argument (1 min)
sections.content: Show why the 'square' condition forces an intersection. By rotating our coordinates, we prove that the 'non-square' set cannot exist without violating topological continuity.
sections.example: An animation of a rectangle morphing into a square as a slider moves across the curve—the 'zero' point is inevitable.

sections.title: Conclusion & Open Frontiers (0.5 min)
sections.content: Summarize the result: For smooth curves, it's proven. Mention that the conjecture for general continuous curves is still a vibrant area of research.
sections.example: A final visual: A digital robot 'finding' the square in a complex landscape, illustrating that topology provides the map, even when the shape is unpredictable.
